extracted.intended_audience: editors, collectors, and scholars of traditional/folk ballads; antiquaries and literary historians
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for collecting, editing, annotating, and publishing traditional ballads: assessing antiquity, documenting provenance and variants, supplying missing verses cautiously, glossing dialect, and providing historical/contextual notes and tune associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document provenance and informant
rubrics_metrics.description: State who communicated the ballad and its source (e.g., 'This ballad was communicated to me by Mr Kirkpatrick Sharpe of Hoddom, who mentions having copied it from an old magazine.'; 'communicated to me by Mr James Hogg').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record collector/reciter names and any notes on how the text was obtained; cite prior collectors or manuscript sources when available to support authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note possible modern corrections vs. ancient character
rubrics_metrics.description: Although it has probably received some modern corrections, the general turn seems to be ancient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing, signal where language or form may have been modernized by transmission; balance acknowledgment of modernizing changes with assessment of the poem's underlying antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gloss dialect and archaic terms with footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explanatory footnotes for obscure or dialect words (e.g., footnotes A–E: 'Plea--Used obliquely for dispute', 'Stout--Through this whole ballad, signifies haughty', 'Scug--shelter or expiate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include short glosses and etymological notes inline or as footnotes so modern readers understand regional/archaic vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of interpolations and patching from other ballads
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering how very apt the most accurate reciters are to patch up one ballad with verses from another, the utmost caution cannot always avoid such errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for verses that may have been borrowed from other poems; exercise caution before attributing such verses to the main text and document any editorial decisions to remove, restore, or relocate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore order and reinstate omitted verses with documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The concluding verses of this ballad were inserted in the copy of Tamlane... They are now restored to their proper place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If restoring verses to their 'proper place' or reordering text, explicitly state the change and the provenance or reasoning for the restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply missing lines/verses only with clear attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Two verses and one line were wanting, which are here supplied from a different Ballad, having a plot somewhat similar. These verses are the 6th and 9th.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filling lacunae, borrow cautiously from closely related variants and clearly note which material is editorially supplied and its source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record variant readings and local recitation differences
rubrics_metrics.description: I can trace it back several generations, but cannot hear of its ever having been in print. I have never heard it with any considerable variation, save that one reciter called the dwelling of the feigned sweetheart, 'Castleswa'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document oral-variant forms, regional naming differences, and any stable/unstable passages across reciters to inform textual decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use internal linguistic/cultural details to help date poems
rubrics_metrics.description: This circumstance marks the antiquity of the poem. While wood was plenty in Scotland, charcoal was the usual fuel in the chambers of the wealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage concrete cultural references (fuel, dress, domestic objects) and archaic lexical items as internal evidence when arguing for relative antiquity or social setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify intertextual references and printed antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: A more sanguine antiquary... might perhaps endeavour to identify this poem with the 'Broom Broom on Hill' mentioned by Lane... The same ballad is quoted by one of the personages in a 'very mery and pythie comedie'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search earlier printed or manuscript sources and contemporary references (plays, chronicles) for parallels or direct citations and cite them when proposing identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide tune/air associations when known
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful air of Cowdenknows is well known and popular. In Ettrick Forest the following words are uniformly adapted to the tune, and seem to be the original ballad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a melody or tune is known, record the air name and note how words are adapted to it; cite published musical editions or oral testimony about tune–text relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace parallels with historical chronicles and motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare, from such old chronicles, has drawn his authority for the last fine scene in King John. But he probably had it from Caxton, who uses nearly the words of the prose chronicle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare ballad motifs with historical chronicles and other literary works to locate possible sources, analogues, or routes of transmission; document these connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize motifs with broader popular belief and superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of this nature are very common in the annals of popular superstition... the wailing of murdered infants had ascended from behind his couch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate motifs (e.g., infant murder, penance, prophecy) within known popular beliefs to explain recurrence and interpret meaning for modern readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit editorial judgments about inclusion even if derivative
rubrics_metrics.description: Although it bears a strong resemblance to that of Earl Richard... yet its intrinsic merit seems to warrant its insertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including a ballad that resembles another, state the editorial rationale (intrinsic merit, local currency, uniqueness) so readers understand selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical/biographical evidence to support or question identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero is more generally termed Lord Ronald; but I willingly follow the authority of an Ettrick Forest copy for calling him Randal; because... I think it not impossible, that the ballad may have originally regarded the death of Thomas Randolph...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh onomastic and historical clues (names, events) against available records; present such identifications as tentative when the evidence is circumstantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide critical commentary on social values and modern reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Such was the readiness, with which, in those times, heroes put their lives in jeopardy... But I doubt whether the fair dames of the present day will think, that the risk of being burned... could be altogether compensated...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer interpretive remarks comparing historical social norms to contemporary sensibilities to help readers contextualize and evaluate problematic or archaic elements.
